title: Neo-Babylonian Empire
capsule: The Neo-Babylonian Empire (626–539 BCE), also called the Chaldean Empire, was the last polity ruled by native Mesopotamian monarchs, founded when Nabopolassar overthrew Assyrian control of Babylon in 626 BCE and in alliance with the Medes destroyed Nineveh in 612 BCE and partitioned the Assyrian Empire. Its greatest ruler, Nebuchadnezzar II (r. 605–562 BCE), defeated Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BCE, conquered Judah and destroyed Jerusalem and the First Temple in 586 BCE, and undertook the rebuilding of Babylon on a monumental scale—the Ishtar Gate, Processional Way, and the legendary Hanging Gardens. The empire fell with striking speed when Cyrus the Great of Persia defeated the last king Nabonidus's forces at Opis in October 539 BCE; Babylon surrendered without a siege and was incorporated into the Achaemenid Empire.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Core Mesopotamian territory and major provincial acquisitions are well documented through cuneiform administrative tablets, Babylonian chronicles, and Biblical sources; frontier zones in Arabia and the Levant and exact border delineations are reconstructed with moderate confidence.
